overview.summary: Nuclear fission supplies firm, around-the-clock electricity that is among the lowest-carbon and lowest-death energy sources ever measured, yet remains contested over its cost, build speed, waste, and catastrophic-accident risk.
overview.scope_covered: Civilian fission for grid electricity: the climate and safety case, lifecycle emissions and death rates, Western vs. Asian build cost and schedule, long-lived waste and disposal, accident and proliferation risk, and the new AI/data-center demand driving a build revival. Covers today's large light-water fleet plus the SMR and Gen-IV bet.
overview.scope_excluded: Nuclear weapons and weapons policy, fusion, naval/space propulsion, medical isotopes, and fossil-vs-renewable debates except where they set nuclear's competitive baseline. Country-by-country energy politics is touched only as evidence on cost and siting, not catalogued.
overview.why_now: A 1970s-80s reactor fleet is aging into retirement just as electricity demand climbs from AI data centers, electrification, and reshoring — the first sustained demand growth in a generation — while climate targets call for firm clean power. Support is near record highs and the partisan gap is the narrowest of any energy source (up 16 points since 2020), though nuclear still trails solar (77%) and wind (68%) in public favor at 59% (Pew, 2025); tech firms are signing reactor restart and SMR deals. The live question is increasingly less whether nuclear is wanted than whether the West can build it on time and on budget.

basics.intro: Six decision-relevant facts that nearly every position on nuclear energy accepts — the shared empirical floor. Five are durable structural figures; one (global share / record generation) is time-sensitive and checked against IEA Electricity 2026 (published Feb 2026), which confirms a new absolute record in 2025 while nuclear's percentage share sits near its multi-decade low. The death rate uses Our World in Data's headline figure (~0.03 deaths/TWh — their Chernobyl + Fukushima toll, the latter already including evacuation-related deaths, over cumulative 1965-2021 generation); a higher ~0.07 appears in some other compilations using broader assumptions, but both leave nuclear in the safest tier with wind and solar. One whole position (Risk-First) does contest these accident tolls as undercounts — noted in Positions — but the mainstream figures here are accepted across the pro and cost-skeptic cases. The build-cost gap is the one shared fact that directly feeds the crux: everyone agrees the West builds far more expensively than South Korea; they disagree on why.

stats.label: Deaths per TWh, lifecycle
stats.note: Among the safest sources — coal 24.6, oil 18.4, gas 2.8, nuclear 0.03, wind 0.04, solar ~0.02 — even counting Chernobyl and Fukushima. Differences among nuclear, wind, and solar are within the uncertainty bands; all are vastly safer than fossil fuels.
stats.source_label: Our World in Data (deaths data through 2021)

stats.label: Lifecycle CO2
stats.note: IPCC AR5 median — among the lowest of any source; coal ~820, gas ~490.

stats.label: Capacity factor
stats.note: Highest of any US source — runs near-continuously; 92.3% in 2024, ~91% in 2025.

stats.label: Share of global electricity
stats.note: Near its lowest share in decades (nuclear peaked around 17-18% in the mid-1990s), yet absolute output set a new record in 2025 (~2,700 TWh, up ~1.2% on 2024's record 2,667 TWh) — demand is growing about as fast as nuclear. Low-emissions sources together reached ~42% of global electricity.
stats.source_label: IEA Electricity 2026; World Nuclear Association (2024 figure)

stats.label: Build cost, West vs. Korea
stats.note: South Korea ~$2,200/kWe overnight vs. Vogtle ~$10,000/kWe overnight (~$35bn for 2.2 GWe; far higher all-in), and generic US new-build >$6,000/kWe — the gap that feeds the central crux. UK's Hinkley Point C reached ~£48bn in Feb 2026, roughly double its approval-era budget.
stats.source_label: IEA/NEA Projected Costs (structural gap); World Nuclear Association, Economics of Nuclear Power (Vogtle/Hinkley)

stats.label: Spent fuel, all-time
stats.note: All spent fuel ever discharged worldwide (~30%, about one-third, reprocessed); high-level waste proper is <1% by volume — it would cover one football field a few metres deep. Volume is not the skeptics' objection: their concern is isolation integrity over 10^4-10^5 years, not how much space it takes.

questions.text: Are runaway Western nuclear costs fixable, or structural?
questions.why: South Korea builds reactors for roughly $2,000-4,000/kW while recent Western projects (Vogtle ~$10,000/kW, Hinkley Point C now ~£48bn) ran years late and billions over. The contest is causal: if the overruns trace to lost supply chains, one-off designs, and stop-start programs, reform and serial building could restore low costs; if they encode genuine democratic safety and regulatory preferences, no process fix removes them. Empirical at root — a factual question about what drives costs — though it shades into values about acceptable caution.

questions.text: Can new nuclear be built fast enough, at scale, to matter for mid-century climate and demand?
questions.why: Solar added ~550-600 GW per year in 2024-2025 while nuclear added single-digit GW net, with new reactor construction not accelerating until the 2030s — an ~80-100x gap in current deployment pace. Advocates argue firm clean power will be needed regardless of how fast it scales and that build rates can ramp; skeptics argue the timelines and historical build records make a material mid-century contribution implausible. Achievable build rates and supply-chain capacity are measurable in principle; the disagreement is over forecasts, not values.

questions.text: Is nuclear waste solved in principle but unsolved in practice?
questions.why: Deep geological disposal is widely regarded as technically sound, and Finland's Onkalo is moving into operation as the first repository for civilian spent fuel — yet decades in, most countries still have no sited repository and the only long-operating deep store (WIPP) takes military transuranic waste, not spent fuel. Skeptics (Ramana among them) further argue repositories carry real long-timescale failure risk from canister corrosion and shifting geology, so the engineering is not as settled as proponents claim. The dispute is partly factual but turns on a normative judgment — how much an unsolved-in-practice siting-and-trust problem, and irreducible deep-time uncertainty, should count as the problem being unsolved.

questions.text: Do nuclear's catastrophic and intergenerational tail risks warrant treating it differently from ordinary energy risks?
questions.why: By lifecycle deaths per unit of energy nuclear is among the safest sources, yet its harms are concentrated, dreaded, and span generations — rare meltdowns, proliferation pathways, and waste that outlasts the institutions meant to guard it. (Some skeptics also contest the death statistics themselves, holding the Chernobyl and Fukushima tolls are undercounted.) Even where the figures are agreed, people differ on whether low-probability, high-consequence, long-tail risks deserve a special precautionary standard or should be weighed on the same expected-value terms as any other hazard — a normative choice no dataset resolves.

questions.text: Is firm, dispatchable nuclear necessary for a deep-decarbonized grid, or can renewables plus storage do the job alone?
questions.why: System models in the Jenkins/MIT vein find that adding firm low-carbon sources, including nuclear, lowers the total cost and risk of reaching zero emissions, while Jacobson-style analyses argue 100% wind-water-solar with storage and transmission is feasible — with Clack and others disputing those assumptions. Both camps largely agree the first ~80% is straightforward; the fight is over the last stretch to fully firm, weather-proof reliability. A modeling and engineering question; disagreement turns on cost assumptions and system constraints, not ethics.

questions.text: Is nuclear the most cost-effective place to spend the marginal climate and energy dollar?
questions.why: Abatement costs are highly context-dependent — relicensing existing reactors or well-sited solar can be near zero per ton avoided, while new-build nuclear is far costlier and renewables displacing already-clean power can be effectively infinite. Even sharing those numbers, ranking the marginal dollar depends on what one is optimizing for — speed, firmness, option value, equity, or least cost — so it resolves to a choice of objective. The cost figures are empirical, but 'most cost-effective place to spend' embeds a goal and a portfolio strategy.

positions.name: Climate Pragmatist
positions.steelman: Nuclear is the only proven, scaled, firm low-carbon power we have — closing it just burns gas instead.
positions.description: Decarbonization is a race against time, and nuclear is the only zero-carbon source that has ever powered a modern grid around the clock at scale: it and hydro already supply roughly three-quarters of the world's low-carbon electricity, and over fifty years nuclear alone has avoided more than 60 gigatonnes of CO2. Unlike weather-dependent wind and solar, the existing fleet delivers firm output — U.S. reactors ran at about a 92% capacity factor in 2024, the highest of any source — at lifecycle emissions (~12 g CO2/kWh, per the IPCC) among the lowest measured. The lesson from Germany's 2023 phase-out and the fights over Diablo Canyon is blunt: when a reactor shuts early, fossil gas and coal fill the gap and emissions rise, so retiring carbon-free plants is running in place on climate. The cheapest, fastest climate megawatt is therefore the one already on the grid — keep the fleet running, relicense it, and build more — because there is no credible path to climate stabilization that does not include a substantial role for nuclear.
positions.proponents: James Hansen, Kerry Emanuel, Ken Caldeira, Tom Wigley, Stewart Brand, IEA, Clean Air Task Force
positions.representative_note: climate scientist who broke with much of the green movement to back nuclear, co-author of the 2013 open letter arguing there is "no credible path to climate stabilization" without it.

positions.name: New-Nuclear Advocate
positions.steelman: Nuclear's cost problem isn't physics — it's lost repetition; serial builds, SMRs, and Gen-IV turn megaprojects into factory products.
positions.description: Nuclear is not inherently expensive — the West simply forgot how to build it. When reactors are built as a standardized fleet rather than one-off megaprojects, costs fall: France's Messmer plan delivered 58 near-identical reactors in roughly six years each, and Korea's APR1400 — exported on schedule to the UAE's Barakah plant — still builds at about a quarter of recent Western per-kW costs. The next leap is industrial: small modular and Gen-IV designs (TerraPower's Natrium, NuScale, Last Energy's factory-kit micro-reactors) move fabrication into factories where learning-by-doing compounds, so the fifth and tenth units cost far less than the first. The Western cost blowouts at Vogtle, Hinkley Point C, and Flamanville are symptoms of stop-start programs and atrophied supply chains, not proof that the technology can't be cheap — restore continuity and serial production and the price falls.
positions.proponents: TerraPower, NuScale, Last Energy (Energy Impact Center / Bret Kugelmass), Jigar Shah, U.S. Department of Energy
positions.representative_note: CEO building the Natrium Gen-IV reactor in Wyoming, who argues each plant can run "half the cost per gigawatt" with the first unit costing more than the fifth or sixth as serial production compounds.

positions.name: Cost Skeptic
positions.steelman: The climate is a race against the clock and the budget, and nuclear loses both.
positions.description: Climate progress is bounded by money and time, so the only honest test is carbon saved per dollar per year — and on that test nuclear is the worst major option. Lazard's 2025 figures put new nuclear at roughly $140-220/MWh against $37-86 for onshore wind and $38/MWh and up for utility solar, and a new reactor takes about 90 months to lead-in versus 40 for wind and solar. Three-quarters of a plant's cost is the ordinary thermal-plant machinery that stopped getting cheaper decades ago, which is why nuclear has never ridden a learning curve while solar, wind, and storage keep halving — so by the time SMRs could mass-produce, their rivals will be twice cheaper again. Vogtle and Hinkley Point C (now near £48bn and roughly double their original budgets) aren't bad luck; they are what the technology costs, and every dollar parked in them is carbon that cheaper, faster options would already have cut. This isn't anti-nuclear ideology — it's portfolio discipline: buy the most decarbonization you can with the dollars and years you actually have.
positions.proponents: Amory Lovins, Mark Z. Jacobson, BloombergNEF analysts
positions.representative_note: RMI physicist who argues costly, slow nuclear is counterproductive for climate because each dollar displaces far less carbon per year than the efficiency and renewables it crowds out.

positions.name: Risk-First Skeptic
positions.steelman: Some risks are too catastrophic and too long-lived to gamble on — and a renewable grid fails far more gracefully.
positions.description: Meltdowns, weapons proliferation, and waste that stays lethal for longer than any state has ever existed are not the kind of risks you can price, insure, or average away — a single bad day at one reactor can poison a region for generations, and no institution can credibly promise stewardship across 100,000 years. And the routine-safety statistics are themselves contested: independent estimates of Chernobyl's long-run toll (TORCH ~30,000-60,000; Greenpeace far higher) dwarf the official count, and Fukushima's mass evacuation killed and displaced thousands that per-TWh figures barely capture. Proliferation is not incidental but first-order: every expansion of enrichment and reprocessing spreads latent bomb-making capability, the civilian-military line is thin and has been crossed before — which is why a disarmament scholar treats reactor proliferation as a central cost, not a footnote. A nuclear system is brittle by design — highly centralized, unforgiving of human error, and a standing target — where the cost of failure is unacceptable; a distributed grid of solar, wind, and storage is the opposite, failing contained rather than catastrophic, because when a panel or battery fails the lights stay on elsewhere. In the face of irreversible, intergenerational harm, deep caution isn't fear — it's the responsible default, and we have a safer path that doesn't demand the bet.
positions.proponents: M.V. Ramana, Arnie Gundersen, Mycle Schneider (World Nuclear Industry Status Report), Frank von Hippel, Greenpeace
positions.representative_note: UBC disarmament scholar; his 2024 book "Nuclear is Not the Solution" argues meltdown, proliferation, and intractable waste rule nuclear out. (His own case also leads with cost and time, overlapping the Cost Skeptic, with safety and proliferation as reinforcing pillars.)

crux.lead: Nearly everyone agrees nuclear is low-carbon and statistically safe per unit of energy — the open fight is two-fold: whether the West can build it cheaply and fast enough to matter, and how much weight its rare, dreaded, long-tail risks deserve.
crux.lead_highlight: cheaply and fast enough to matter
crux.subtitle: The ~12 g CO2/kWh is essentially undisputed, and the routine death rate is low by every mainstream measure (OWID ~0.03/TWh, even counting Chernobyl and Fukushima) — though the risk-first camp contests those accident tolls as undercounts and, more deeply, holds that an averaged death rate is the wrong lens for catastrophic, irreversible, hundred-thousand-year harm. What even skeptics grant is that nuclear is not a high-carbon source — so the real fight is not climate but two entangled things. First, an empirical one: are the West's cost-and-schedule blowouts (Vogtle, Hinkley) a contingent failure of lost supply chains and one-off designs that serial building and SMRs can fix, or a structural feature no reform removes — and even if fixed, is firm nuclear actually needed when renewables-plus-storage may cover the last stretch? Second, a values one: how much a low-probability, high-consequence, multi-generational risk should count. The first is where the two pro cases meet the cost skeptic; the second is where caution diverges even if the price falls. Both are live — neither is closed.
crux.empirical: Then it turns on two measurable things. What actually drives Western cost — if lost repetition and stop-start programs, serial fleets like Korea's restore low prices and nuclear scales; if the overruns are intrinsic to the thermal machinery, cheaper, faster renewables win the marginal climate dollar regardless. And, even granting cheap firm power, whether a renewables-plus-storage grid can hold the last stretch to fully reliable without it, and whether nuclear can deploy fast enough to matter by mid-century given an ~80-100x current build-rate gap. Causal questions that better build data and system models could settle.
crux.values: Then it turns on how catastrophic, irreversible, intergenerational risk should count — weighed on the same expected-value terms as any hazard (where nuclear's death rate already wins), or held to a special precautionary standard for dread, for accident tolls the camp argues are undercounted, and for a proliferation channel whose size is itself partly contested. A choice no dataset closes.

actions.title: Our World in Data — Nuclear Energy
actions.description: The shared-facts baseline: lifecycle emissions, deaths per TWh, and nuclear's share of global electricity — the figures every position cites.

actions.title: Clean Air Task Force — Nuclear Scaling Initiative
actions.description: Pushes nuclear as proven firm clean power, targeting 50+ GW built globally per year by the 2030s. Donate via 'Ways to Give.'

actions.title: Good Energy Collective
actions.description: Builds the progressive, climate-justice case for nuclear as part of the broader climate agenda. 4-star Charity Navigator; Giving Green-recognized.

actions.title: Nuclear Innovation Alliance
actions.description: Non-partisan 'think-and-do' tank working to make advanced reactors deployable — policy, licensing reform, deployment tracking.

actions.title: Generation Atomic — Atomic Ambassador
actions.description: A ~4-hour training, then join a volunteer team — legislative outreach, fact-finding, or community education — to defend at-risk plants and pass pro-nuclear law.

actions.title: RMI (Rocky Mountain Institute)
actions.description: Research and deployment for the renewables-efficiency-electrification path — the case that the marginal clean dollar buys more elsewhere.

actions.title: Beyond Nuclear — Take Action
actions.description: Campaigns to phase out nuclear power on safety, waste, and intergenerational-risk grounds. Action alerts plus an ActBlue donate option.

actions.title: NIRS — Nuclear Information and Resource Service
actions.description: The 'nuclear-free, carbon-free' networking hub since 1978; ~82% of funds go to program work. Donate or join a campaign.

actions.title: Comment on NRC reactor rulemaking
actions.description: How the public weighs in on Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules and licensing — the front door for shaping advanced-reactor and safety rules on regulations.gov.

actions.title: Attend a plant relicensing hearing
actions.description: When an aging plant seeks license renewal, the NRC holds public meetings near the site and affected residents can petition to intervene.

issues: TILT (crux, most significant) — The Crux declares the value/risk axis essentially conceded, which editorializes the one anti-nuclear position toward 'mostly resolved.' subtitle: 'even the risk-first case concedes nuclear isn't uniquely deadly day-to-day. So the headline "is nuclear good for the climate?" is already settled common ground.' and lead_highlight frames the whole fight as merely 'built cheaply and fast enough to matter.' This collapses a genuine value disagreement (how to weight catastrophic/intergenerational/proliferation risk) into a near-settled footnote. A real Risk-First proponent does NOT concede the substance — they concede only the day-to-day death rate while holding that tail risk + proliferation are exactly what the death rate cannot buy down. The crux states this in 'values' but the lead/subtitle override it by pre-announcing the question settled. This is a house tilt toward the pro frame.

MISATTRIBUTED CORE FACT (basics, serious — undermines the whole 'shared floor carries it' strategy) — The Deaths/TWh stat and its intro misattribute 0.07 to Our World in Data. OWID's current HEADLINE figure for nuclear is ~0.03 (their stated method: 433 Chernobyl + 2,314 Fukushima deaths / 96,876 TWh 1965-2021 = 0.0284, rounds to 0.03; verified on ourworldindata.org/nuclear-energy and the death-rates grapher). 0.07 is a DIFFERENT methodology (it appears in derivative/Sovacool-style compilations), not OWID's current value. The draft's claim 'reconciled to Our World in Data's current values, which now place nuclear at 0.07 (revised upward to include Fukushima evacuation-related deaths)' is factually wrong about what OWID currently publishes. Note also the original seed used 0.03 with this same OWID URL — the draft changed the number but kept the OWID attribution.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY (basics) — The stat note reads 'coal 24.6, gas 2.8, nuclear 0.07, solar 0.02' and then says nuclear is 'still in the safest tier with wind and solar.' At 0.07, nuclear is 3.5x solar (0.02) and ~1.75x wind (0.04 per OWID) — it is still very safe, but presenting 0.07 while asserting parity with solar/wind is internally inconsistent. With the correct 0.03, the 'safest tier with wind and solar' claim holds cleanly. The chosen number actively works against the sentence it sits in.

PROPONENT-LIST RIGOR ASYMMETRY (positions) — Risk-First Skeptic proponents = 'M.V. Ramana, Amory Lovins, Arnie Gundersen, M. V. Ramana, Mycle Schneider, Greenpeace.' Two defects: (a) M.V. Ramana is listed TWICE (as 'M.V. Ramana' and 'M. V. Ramana') — a duplication the pro positions don't have; (b) Amory Lovins is DOUBLE-ASSIGNED — he anchors Cost Skeptic (correctly: representative_name = Amory Lovins) and is also dropped into Risk-First. Lovins is a cost/soft-energy-path figure, not primarily a dread-risk/precautionary thinker; putting him in both blurs the two skeptic positions and weakens the Risk-First steelman's distinct identity. The pro positions (Pragmatist, Advocate) have clean, role-appropriate proponent lists, so the anti side reads as comparatively less rigorously curated.

WHY_NOW OMISSION CREATES A PRO-LEAN (plan) — why_now says 'Support is near record highs with the narrowest partisan gap of any energy source ... the decisive question is no longer whether nuclear is wanted but whether the West can build it.' Verified accurate on support (~59-60% favor, Pew/Gallup 2025) and gap (17 pts, narrowest). BUT it omits the directly relevant fact that nuclear remains the LEAST favored of the clean options — solar 77%, wind 68%, nuclear 59% (Pew, May 2025). 'No longer whether nuclear is wanted' overstates public enthusiasm by dropping that nuclear still trails its main clean rivals. This is selective emphasis that favors the pro frame.

PREVALENCE WEIGHTING TILT (plan/positions) — Pro positions: Climate Pragmatist 85, New-Nuclear Advocate 68 (sum 153). Skeptic: Cost Skeptic 72. Anti: Risk-First Skeptic 40. The pro lean in PREVALENCE is defensible as honest non-balance given near-record support and expert/IPCC consensus — that is the rule working correctly, NOT false balance. The concern is calibration: Risk-First at 40 reflects elite/expert opinion more than public opinion, where ~40% still do not favor more nuclear and safety/waste concerns remain mainstream. Combined with the crux pre-declaring the risk question settled, the cumulative effect across plan + crux is a perceptible house lean. Flag as a tilt to correct in framing, not a demand for a 50/50.

ASYMMETRIC SOURCING NOT ACKNOWLEDGED (positions) — Pro positions cite industry + research orgs (TerraPower, NuScale, DOE, IEA, Clean Air Task Force); Risk-First's named org is Greenpeace (advocacy tier). Per the project's own tiering rule (primary/peer-reviewed > journalism > advocacy), leaning the anti position on an advocacy org while the pro positions get research/industry bodies is an unflagged rigor asymmetry. Defensible if intentional, but it currently reads as the anti side being sourced more weakly.

issues: POSITION 4 (Risk-First Skeptic) — steelman is softened in a pro-nuclear direction; its real proponents would NOT endorse it as written. The body concedes 'We don't need to prove nuclear is uniquely deadly day-to-day' and the crux asserts 'even the risk-first case concedes nuclear isn't uniquely deadly day-to-day.' This is the single biggest fidelity failure: the actual #1 empirical claim of this camp is that the casualty figures are UNDERCOUNTED, not conceded. Two of the listed proponents prove it — Greenpeace posits a Chernobyl toll of 93,000–200,000 and the TORCH report 30,000–60,000, vs. the official ~4,000; the camp also argues Fukushima's ~2,300+ evacuation/displacement deaths and long-run harms are undercounted. The draft deletes this claim and replaces it with a concession the proponents explicitly reject. (Verified: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deaths_due_to_the_Chernobyl_disaster; thebulletin.org/2026/03/counting-the-dead-at-fukushima/.)
POSITION 4 — proponents list has a duplication bug: 'M.V. Ramana, Amory Lovins, Arnie Gundersen, M. V. Ramana, Mycle Schneider, Greenpeace' lists Ramana TWICE ('M.V. Ramana' and 'M. V. Ramana').

POSITION 4 — Amory Lovins is miscast: he appears as a proponent of BOTH Cost Skeptic (3) and Risk-First (4). Lovins's signature position is the cost/opportunity-cost argument (Position 3); he explicitly rests his case on economics, not on dread/precaution/catastrophe. Listing him under Risk-First misrepresents him and blurs the two positions' distinctiveness.

POSITION 4 — the representative (M.V. Ramana) is mismatched to how the position is framed. Ramana's own thesis LEADS with 'cost and time' ('fails the two key tests for any climate solution: cost and time'), with accidents/waste/proliferation as the reinforcing case. But Position 4 is framed as pure precaution that needs no cost argument ('We don't need to prove nuclear is uniquely deadly... we only need to take seriously the tail risk'), ceding all cost/time to Position 3. The representative's actual lead argument is attached to the wrong position. (Verified: sppga.ubc.ca Q&A; versobooks.com/products/3013.)

POSITION 4 — proliferation is the position's load-bearing pillar (its representative is a DISARMAMENT scholar) but is rendered as a single throwaway clause ('the proliferation channel it opens'). The strongest version — commercial enrichment/reprocessing creating latent weapons capability, the historical power-to-weapons pathway Ramana built his career on — is absent. Underweighting it is a steelman weakness.

POSITION 4 — its ground on waste is conceded away in adjacent sections, weakening the steelman. Basics frames high-level waste as trivial ('one football field a few metres deep') and Questions frames disposal as 'solved in principle' and even RECLASSIFIES the waste question from value→empirical on the premise the engineering is 'broadly accepted as technically sound.' Risk-First proponents (Ramana explicitly) reject this: he argues geological repositories 'carry a high risk of failure due to long-term... geological conditions.' Asserting disposal is settled presupposes the pro-nuclear answer and strips the skeptic's contested ground.

CRUX — the lead and subtitle overclaim shared ground by attributing concessions the risk-first camp does not make: 'The 12 g/kWh and the 0.07 deaths per TWh are not in dispute' and 'the headline is nuclear good for the climate? is already settled common ground.' Honest non-balance requires noting that the safety/death-toll figure is itself contested by one whole camp; presenting it as universally conceded puts words in the skeptics' mouths.

POSITIONS 1–3 are NOT problems — flagged here only to scope the audit: their steelmen are high-fidelity and in-voice, and three checkable proponent claims verified accurate (Hansen 2013 letter 'no credible path to climate stabilization that does not include a substantial role for nuclear power' is verbatim; Levesque's 'half the cost per gigawatt' / 'first plant more expensive than the fifth or sixth' is accurate; Ramana's book title is exact). No fixes needed for 1–3 beyond the optional one below.
fixes: Position 4 steelman/description — restore the contested-casualty claim instead of conceding it. Replace 'We don't need to prove nuclear is uniquely deadly day-to-day to reject it; we only need to take seriously the tail risk and the proliferation channel it opens' with something like: 'And the routine-safety statistics are themselves contested — independent estimates of Chernobyl's long-run toll (TORCH ~30,000–60,000; Greenpeace far higher) dwarf the official count, and Fukushima's mass evacuation killed and displaced thousands the per-TWh figures barely capture. Even setting the body count aside, the tail risk and the proliferation channel are reason enough.' This keeps the precautionary core but stops surrendering the camp's empirical claim.

Position 4 — give proliferation its own load-bearing sentence, e.g.: 'Every expansion of enrichment and reprocessing spreads latent bomb-making capability; the civilian–military line is thin and has been crossed before, which is why a disarmament scholar treats reactor proliferation as a first-order, not incidental, cost.'

Position 4 proponents — fix the list to: 'M.V. Ramana, Arnie Gundersen, Mycle Schneider, Frank von Hippel, Greenpeace' (remove the duplicate Ramana; drop Lovins to Position 3 only; optionally add a proliferation/accident name like Frank von Hippel or Edwin Lyman). Keep Lovins solely under Cost Skeptic.

Crux lead/subtitle — stop asserting the death rate is undisputed. Change 'The 12 g/kWh and the 0.07 deaths per TWh are not in dispute — even the risk-first case concedes nuclear isn't uniquely deadly day-to-day' to e.g. 'The low lifecycle carbon (~12 g/kWh) is essentially undisputed; the routine death rate is low by every mainstream measure though the risk-first camp contests the accident tolls. What even skeptics grant is that nuclear is not a high-carbon source — so the real fight is not climate but cost, speed, and how to weigh catastrophic risk.'

Questions — reconsider the waste reclassification. Either keep kind=value (the dispute over 'how much the unsited-repository gap counts' is genuinely normative and is the skeptic's ground), or, if kept empirical, add the skeptic's actual claim to the 'why' (long-timescale canister/geology failure risk per Ramana) so the framing isn't one-sided toward 'solved in principle.'

Basics — soften the waste-trivializing note so it doesn't pre-decide Position 4's contested ground: keep the 'football field' volume figure but append that volume is not the skeptics' objection — isolation integrity over 10^4–10^5 years is — so the stat reads as scale, not as 'problem minimized.'

Optional, Position 3 — Lovins's representative_note can be sharpened from 'saves far less carbon per year' to his actual stronger claim that costly, slow nuclear is counterproductive for climate because it displaces less carbon per dollar-year than the alternatives it crowds out (opportunity cost). The description already implies this; the note can match it.

issues: GENERATION FIGURE WRONG (stat: Share of global electricity, note). The note claims absolute output 'hit a record 2,850 TWh in 2025.' Verified sources: world nuclear generation was 2,667 TWh in 2024 (a record, World Nuclear Performance Report 2025, Sept 2025); IEA Electricity 2026 reports 2025 grew ~1.2% over 2024, which yields ~2,700 TWh, not 2,850. The 2,850 figure is ~6% too high and appears in no source. The 'record in 2025' claim itself is correct (IEA Electricity 2026, pub 2026-02-06 confirms a new record), but the specific number is fabricated/overstated.

DEATH-RATE NOTE INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT (stat: Deaths per TWh). The headline 0.07 deaths/TWh for nuclear is CORRECT and current — OWID's safest-sources-of-energy page now computes 0.07 by including Fukushima evacuation-related deaths (~2,314) plus Chernobyl (433) over 1965-2021 generation. Good. BUT the note's comparator 'solar 0.02' is from the OLDER OWID dataset. The same current OWID dataset that yields 0.07 for nuclear lists solar at ~0.04 and wind at ~0.04. The draft mixes a new nuclear figure with an old solar figure, so the ranked comparison is inconsistent within one source.

VOGTLE COST UNDERSTATED (stat: Build cost West vs Korea, note). The note says 'Vogtle ~$8,000' overnight. Verified: Vogtle 3&4 total ~$35bn for 2,234 MWe ≈ $11,391/kW overnight (World Nuclear Association, Economics of Nuclear Power). $8,000 materially understates it. The generic US '>$6,000/kWe overnight' is loosely consistent with EIA's ~$7,821/kWe (2023$) generic estimate, so that part is acceptable, but the Vogtle parenthetical is wrong.

STALE SOURCE FOR BUILD-COST STAT (stat: Build cost West vs Korea). Source cited is IEA/NEA Projected Costs of Generating Electricity 2020 (6 years old) and the URL points to the 2020 edition. The ~$2,200/kWe Korea figure and the ~3x ratio are still broadly defensible/structural, but the Western anchor has moved since 2020 (Hinkley Point C rose to ~£48-50bn as announced Feb 2026 per WNA/Wikipedia). The 'durable=true' tag is reasonable for the gap's existence, but the dollar figures and the parenthetical examples need a current source, not the 2020 report.

UNSOURCED 'lowest in 45+ years' CLAIM (stat: Share of global electricity, note). The 9% share for 2024 is correct (IEA Global Energy Review 2025 / Electricity 2026). But 'Lowest share in 45+ years' is not stated in the cited IEA Electricity 2026 page and is not supported by the provided source. It is plausible (nuclear peaked near 17-18% in the mid-1990s and has declined as the denominator grew) but must be cited or softened. Also the source_url (iea.org/reports/electricity-2026) returns 403 on direct fetch; the report exists and pub date 2026-02-06 is correct, but the share/record claims should be attributed to a verifiable IEA page (executive-summary or supply).

SPENT FUEL FIGURE NEEDS RECONCILING (stat: Spent fuel all-time). The cited IAEA source (2022 radioactive-waste overview) could not be fetched (paywalled/402). Cross-checks: IAEA reports ~390,000 tHM discharged through end-2016 and 'about 400,000 tonnes discharged, ~one-third reprocessed' in general references. ~430 kt for ~2022 is a plausible extrapolation but is not directly confirmed from the cited source, and the note's '~30% reprocessed' should read '~one-third' (~33%) to match IAEA wording. Verify the 430 kt against the actual cited 2022 report or relabel as '~400 kt'.

SOURCE-DATE MISLABEL (stat: Deaths per TWh). source_published is '2024' but OWID's underlying death-rate dataset spans 1965-2021 and the 0.07 nuclear value derives from that cumulative window; the page was last revised more recently. The figure is current/correct, but '2024' as the data vintage is imprecise — cite as OWID (data through 2021, page updated 2024) for honesty.

Stat 'Spent fuel all-time' note: change '~30% reprocessed' to '~one-third reprocessed' to match IAEA. Stat 'Lifecycle CO2' (value 12, IPCC AR5) and 'Capacity factor' (92.3% 2024, ~91% 2025) require NO change — both verified accurate against IPCC AR5 WG3 Annex III (nuclear 12, coal ~820, gas ~490 g CO2e/kWh medians) and EIA capacity-factor data respectively.

Update the basics 'intro' paragraph: it asserts the death figures were 'reconciled to Our World in Data's current values, which now place nuclear at 0.07' — that reconciliation is correct for nuclear but was NOT applied to the solar comparator in the note; after fixing the note, the intro's claim becomes true. Also soften 'verified to the latest IEA Electricity 2026 data' for the share stat so it does not imply the 2,850 TWh figure (now corrected) came from IEA.

issues: CORE VERDICT (crux is a genuine narrowing, NOT false balance): The crux passes its central test. It identifies real settled common ground (low-carbon + historically safe) that all four positions genuinely concede in their own text — including the Risk-First position, whose draft says 'We don't need to prove nuclear is uniquely deadly day-to-day to reject it.' So the crux's claim that 'even the risk-first case concedes nuclear isn't uniquely deadly day-to-day' is faithful, not a strawman. It then narrows to two specific live disagreements and — crucially — treats them ASYMMETRICALLY: the empirical limb says better build data could settle it and names which way each outcome cuts; the values limb says no dataset closes it. That is the opposite of '50/50 both-sides' framing. It also maps each crux to where it sits in the position landscape ('where the two pro cases meet the cost skeptic' vs 'where caution diverges even if the price falls'), which is a real structural insight. The issues below are correctable defects, not a failure of the core narrowing.

BLOCKING — the crux anchors on an unverified/incorrect figure presented as bedrock. The subtitle asserts 'the 0.07 deaths per TWh [is] not in dispute.' Verified against Our World in Data: OWID's published methodology is (433 Chernobyl + 2,314 Fukushima) / 96,876 TWh ≈ 0.028, which OWID rounds to 0.03. The 2,314 Fukushima figure ALREADY includes evacuation-related deaths, so the draft's Basics justification ('OWID now place nuclear at 0.07... revised upward to include Fukushima evacuation-related deaths') is false — there is no such OWID revision. (0.07 does appear in some older/other estimates e.g. Markandya & Wilkinson / Lancet-derived, so it's a real number in the literature, but it is NOT OWID's current value and not 'undisputed.') The crux makes this its uncontested empirical floor; a reviewer who checks finds the foundation wrong. Note the empirical case is unharmed — at 0.03 nuclear's death-rate advantage is even larger — so this is a pure factual-anchor fix.

SUBSTANTIVE — the empirical limb over-narrows by collapsing the whole factual disagreement into 'what drives Western cost.' The draft itself carries six questions, two of which are NOT cost-of-nuclear questions: Q5 'is firm dispatchable nuclear necessary for a deep-decarbonized grid, or can renewables+storage do it alone' (the Jacobson vs Clack/Jenkins fight — verified real and live) and Q2 'can it be built fast enough/at scale to matter.' The crux's empirical text says 'if serial fleets restore low prices... nuclear scales,' treating cheapness as sufficient for the pro case to win. But the draft's own Q5 holds that even cheap firm power is contested as NECESSARY, and Q2 holds that even fixable unit costs may not yield a material mid-century contribution given build rates (~80-100x current deployment gap vs solar). So the crux folds a second genuine empirical axis (system-need + deployment-speed) into the single cost axis. Leading with cost is defensible — it is the sharpest fulcrum — but the crux currently implies cost is the entire empirical ballgame, which under-represents the topic's own contested terrain.

MINOR — the values limb mis-sorts proliferation as purely values. The crux puts 'dread and proliferation that no safety statistic can buy down' wholly in the values limb. Whether civilian nuclear expansion measurably raises weapons-proliferation risk has an empirical component (it is partly a factual claim about enrichment/reprocessing pathways and the historical record), which the crux flattens into a non-factual 'dread' bucket. Low severity but it slightly muddies the otherwise-clean empirical/values cut.

CONTEXT (not a crux defect, but the crux inherits it) — the cost-gap magnitude in Basics understates reality, which weakens the empirical fulcrum the crux leans on. Basics frames it as '~3x' (US >$6,000/kWe, 'Vogtle ~$8,000', Korea ~$2,200). Verified: Vogtle overnight is ~$10,000/kW (all-in ~$17,500/kW per unit); Korea ~$2,200/kW overnight. The real overnight gap is ~4-5x (and ~8x all-in), not 3x. The crux doesn't cite a multiple so its logic survives, but since the crux's whole empirical limb rests on 'the West builds far more expensively than Korea,' the under-stated gap in Basics quietly undercuts the crux's strongest evidence.
fixes: Fix the 0.07 anchor. In crux.subtitle replace 'the 0.07 deaths per TWh are not in dispute' with the verified figure and a tier-aware hedge, e.g.: 'The ~12 g CO2/kWh and a death rate in the safest tier (OWID ~0.03/TWh, even counting Chernobyl and Fukushima) are not in dispute'. Do NOT assert a single contested number as undisputed. Correspondingly fix Basics: set the Deaths/TWh stat value to 0.03 (or 0.02-0.03), update the ranked note to 'coal 24.6, gas 2.8, nuclear ~0.03, solar/wind ~0.04', and DELETE the false claim in the Basics intro that OWID 'revised upward to 0.07 to include Fukushima evacuation-related deaths' (the 2,314 figure already includes them). Source: https://ourworldindata.org/safest-sources-of-energy (last updated 2022).

Broaden the empirical limb so it doesn't reduce to cost alone. Revise crux.empirical to name the two-step empirical contest, e.g.: 'Then it turns on two measurable things: what actually drives Western cost — if lost repetition and stop-start programs, serial fleets like Korea's restore low prices; if intrinsic to the thermal machinery, cheaper renewables win the marginal dollar — and, even granting cheap firm power, whether a renewables-plus-storage grid can hold the last stretch to fully reliable without it. Both are causal questions better build data and system models could settle.' This keeps cost as the lead fulcrum while honoring Q2/Q5 so the crux matches the draft's own contested terrain.

Optionally split proliferation cleanly. In crux.values, either keep proliferation but flag its empirical seam (e.g. '...a special precautionary standard for dread — and for a proliferation channel whose size is itself partly contested'), or drop proliferation from the values sentence and let it live in the positions. Either removes the mis-sort.

Strengthen the cost fulcrum in Basics (feeds the crux). Update the 'Build cost, West vs. Korea' stat from '~3x' to '~4-5x overnight (8x all-in)': Korea ~$2,200/kWe overnight vs Vogtle ~$10,000/kWe overnight (~$17,500/kWe all-in per unit). Sources: World Nuclear Association economics page and IEA/NEA Projected Costs; Vogtle all-in widely reported ~$35bn for 2,234 MWe. This makes the empirical limb's premise ('the West builds far more expensively') land with its true magnitude.

No change needed to the crux's core structure, the settled-common-ground claim, the 'Risk-First concedes day-to-day safety' characterization, or the empirical-vs-values asymmetry — all verified accurate and fair. After the four fixes above, this crux is a clean pass.

plan_positions.name: Climate Pragmatist
plan_positions.one_line: The only proven, scaled, firm low-carbon power we have — keep the fleet running and build more, because losing it raises emissions.

plan_positions.name: New-Nuclear Advocate
plan_positions.one_line: The cost problem is solvable: serial builds, SMRs, and Gen-IV designs turn megaprojects into factory products, as Korea and France already show.

plan_positions.name: Cost Skeptic
plan_positions.one_line: Too slow and too expensive to be the rational marginal climate dollar — solar, wind, and storage keep cheapening on a curve nuclear has never shown.

plan_positions.name: Risk-First Skeptic
plan_positions.one_line: Meltdowns, proliferation, and waste that outlasts institutions are not ordinary risks; deep caution is warranted and a renewable grid fails more gracefully.
